opus-5.5.text:
Well, I've been somewhat of a skeptic about NISQ applications for a while now, and I think the evidence so far has mostly borne that skepticism out. When John Preskill coined the term "NISQ" back in 2018, the hope was that, even before we had full fault tolerance, devices with fifty to a few hundred noisy qubits might do something useful: simulate chemistry, solve optimization problems, help with machine learning. And what we've seen instead is that NISQ devices have been great for one thing in particular, which is demonstrating quantum supremacy, or quantum advantage if you prefer: doing sampling tasks that are hard for classical computers to simulate. I was involved in some of the theory behind that, with random circuit sampling and boson sampling, so I'm happy those experiments happened. They told us something real about the world, namely that you can control these systems well enough to get outside the regime that classical computers can easily follow.

But "useful" is a different question. With things like variational algorithms, QAOA for optimization, VQE for chemistry, the problem is twofold. First, the noise kills you: after a certain circuit depth, your output is basically indistinguishable from random, and the depth you can reach without error correction is shallow. Second, and this is the part people sometimes underrate, classical algorithms keep getting better. Every time someone has claimed a NISQ advantage on a practical problem, classical people, tensor network folks and so on, have often come back within months and said, "We can do that on a laptop," or at least on a cluster. That's a healthy scientific process, but it's not kind to the hype.

So my honest assessment is that the most likely path to real economic value from quantum computing goes through error correction. And the encouraging news is that error correction has been progressing faster than many of us expected. We've seen logical qubits that actually outperform the physical qubits they're made from, error rates going below threshold, and multiple hardware platforms, superconducting, trapped ions, neutral atoms, all making serious progress. If I had to place bets, I'd say the first truly compelling applications will be simulating quantum physics and chemistry, which was Feynman's original vision, and then eventually Shor's algorithm, which is the reason we all need to move to post-quantum cryptography sooner rather than later.

Could there be some narrow NISQ application that turns out to be genuinely useful, for instance certified randomness, which is something I've worked on? Yes, I think that's one of the more plausible candidates, because it leverages exactly the thing NISQ devices are good at, which is sampling hard distributions. But as a general-purpose engine for business value before error correction, I'd be cautious. I'd tell people: don't believe a claimed quantum speedup until you've seen the strongest classical competitors take their best shot at it.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare pre-transistor classical computers with quantum computing before error correction.

r002.rationale: It names quantum simulation as a likely compelling application after error correction, while saying a narrow pre-error-correction candidate could be certified randomness.

r003.rationale: It separates scientifically meaningful sampling demonstrations from practical usefulness and economic value, describing the latter as a higher bar.

r004.rationale: It is skeptical about useful pre-error-correction applications and says the most likely path to real economic value goes through error correction.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I've been fairly skeptical about this for years, and I'd say my skepticism has mostly held up, though with some important caveats. Let me try to lay out how I think about it.

The whole premise of the NISQ era, which was John Preskill's term, was the hope that even before you have fault tolerance, you could find some problem where a noisy device with, say, a hundred or a few hundred qubits does something useful that you can't do classically. And the thing people need to understand is that there are really two separate questions hiding in there. One is, can you demonstrate a quantum speedup at all, for anything? And the other is, can you do it for something anyone actually cares about? Those have had very different trajectories.

On the first question, I think the answer is now a pretty clear yes. The random circuit sampling experiments, starting with Google in 2019 and continuing since then, did establish that you can run a quantum computation that would be extraordinarily expensive to simulate classically. There was a back-and-forth for a few years where classical algorithms kept catching up, tensor network methods and so on, and the quantum experiments kept getting bigger and less noisy, and at this point I'd say the quantum side has won that particular race, at least for sampling tasks. But sampling from a random circuit is not useful. It's not even clear how you'd use it as a certified randomness source without a lot of additional work, which is something I've actually spent time on.

On the second question, useful NISQ applications, I think the honest assessment is that it's been disappointing relative to the hype of five or six years ago. The candidate applications were things like variational quantum eigensolvers for chemistry, QAOA for optimization, and various quantum machine learning proposals. And what happened with a lot of them is that when people looked carefully, either the classical competition turned out to be much stronger than assumed, or the quantum version needed so many gates that noise wiped out the advantage, or there was a dequantization result showing you could do the same thing classically. The quantum machine learning stuff especially suffered from that last problem.

Where I've become somewhat more optimistic is on a narrower thing, which is quantum simulation of quantum systems. If you want to simulate the dynamics of a spin system or a lattice model, that's the most natural thing for a quantum computer to do, and there you don't need a cleverly designed algorithm fighting against a classical heuristic. You're just doing the thing the device naturally does. There have been experiments from IBM, from Quantinuum, from Google, that get into regimes where classical methods genuinely struggle. Now, whether those count as useful depends on whether a condensed matter physicist would actually learn something they couldn't learn otherwise, and I think that's still an open question, but it's at least a plausible path.

The other thing that's changed the picture is that fault tolerance stopped being a distant abstraction. Once Google demonstrated a logical qubit with error rates going down as the code distance went up, and once Quantinuum and others started showing logical operations on small numbers of encoded qubits, the question shifted. It went from "what can we do with noisy qubits forever" to "what can we do with noisy qubits for the next few years while we build the real thing." And honestly, if the real thing is coming on a timescale of a decade or less, then I'd rather the field pour its effort into getting there than into squeezing out marginal NISQ wins.

So my overall view is something like this. NISQ delivered on the science, meaning it showed quantum computational advantage is real and not just a theorist's fantasy. It mostly did not deliver on applications, and I think the people who were promising commercial value from fifty noisy qubits were doing the field a disservice. And the most interesting remaining NISQ-ish niche is physics simulation, which may end up being a kind of bridge to the error-corrected era rather than a destination in itself.

r002.rationale: It calls quantum simulation the area where the speaker has become more optimistic and the most interesting remaining NISQ-like niche, describing it as a plausible path to advantage where classical methods struggle.

r003.rationale: It separates demonstrating a quantum speedup from doing something useful, says NISQ showed scientific advantage but mostly did not deliver applications, and criticizes promises of commercial value from noisy qubits.

r004.rationale: The response favors building toward fault tolerance, but does not express greater confidence that speedups will be achieved after error correction than before it.

astra-6.text:
I’m cautiously skeptical. The question is not just whether a noisy quantum device can do something that’s hard to simulate classically. It’s whether it can do something useful, and do it better than the best classical methods. That’s a much higher bar.

The difficulty is that, without error correction, you can only run a computation for so long before noise overwhelms the result. A lot of the proposed applications involve these hybrid quantum-classical algorithms, where you run a small quantum circuit and then have a classical optimizer adjust it. Those are worth exploring, but we don’t have strong evidence that they’ll deliver a practical advantage. And classical algorithms are a moving target.

If there’s an early useful application, quantum simulation—learning about molecules or materials—seems like a natural place to look. But even there, you have to ask whether the device can reach a regime that’s both scientifically interesting and beyond classical methods.

So I’d be delighted to see useful applications before fault tolerance. I just wouldn’t make the case for quantum computing depend on that happening. Error correction is what gives us a systematic way to scale up the computations we know quantum computers could be good at.

r001.rationale: The response does not use pre-transistor classical computers as an analogy.

r002.rationale: It names quantum simulation as a natural place to look for an early useful application and asks whether it can reach beyond classical methods.

r003.rationale: It contrasts useful applications with scientifically interesting results, but does not specifically distinguish commercially useful advantage from scientifically interesting advantage over classical computation.

r004.rationale: It says error correction offers a systematic way to scale computations, but does not clearly express greater confidence in speedups after error correction than before it.

sol-6.1.text:
I would say that it’s still an open question, and I’m skeptical of confident claims on either side. We know that quantum computers can, in principle, outperform classical computers for certain problems. But that doesn’t tell us whether a noisy device with a limited number of qubits can solve a useful problem better than the best classical methods.

The difficulty is that noise limits how many operations you can perform before the quantum information becomes unreliable. And classical algorithms are a moving target: when someone proposes a near-term quantum application, people often find better classical ways to tackle it.

Quantum simulation seems to me like one of the most plausible places to look, because you’re using one quantum system to understand another. But even there, you have to establish an advantage at a scale and accuracy that someone actually cares about. So I think these experiments are worth doing. I just wouldn’t make useful quantum computing depend on the hope that we can avoid error correction.
